title: What a Canadian salary guide really says

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: If you work in tech in Canada, how does your pay compare to engineering, or to the same job in another city? Antoine went looking for an answer in a 2023 salary guide from a recruitment firm.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: Where did the data come from?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: From a GitHub project called Salary, where the guide's text was already extracted. Nineteen thousand three hundred eighty-seven rows of salary ranges, across fifty-six named regions. Every cell was tagged by heading level, so he could rebuild the original tables.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: And rebuilding them took some care?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: It did. Most tables have entry, mid and senior columns, but finance and HR tables are organised by years of experience or by company size, and some industrial jobs are quoted per hour. Reading each table on its own terms is what makes the numbers comparable.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So once it's read properly, what does the guide say?

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Technology pays the most. The median mid-level figure is ninety-seven thousand two hundred dollars, about fifteen thousand above engineering. And across jobs, senior pay is about one point three times entry pay.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: That's the interesting part. For the same developer or architect role, Montréal, Toronto, Vancouver and Calgary land within about ten percent of each other. The gap between cities is smaller than people often assume.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: He's careful there. Each region lists its own set of jobs, so a provincial median compares different baskets of jobs rather than the same job. Alberta comes first, but that mostly reflects which roles are listed.

lines.speaker: B
lines.text: So these are quoted ranges, not actual paycheques.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Right. They show what a recruitment firm quotes, which is still a useful map of the market.

lines.speaker: A
lines.text: Compare the same job across places, and read each table the way it was built. The full write-up has the charts by job family, province and city.
